evidence.intree_statement: Class IsCartesianProduct (x y z : C) := { fork' {a} (f : a ~> x) (g : a ~> y) : a ~> z; exl' : z ~> x; exr' : z ~> y; fork'_respects : ∀ a, Proper (equiv ==> equiv ==> equiv) (@fork' a); ump_product {a} (f : a ~> x) (g : a ~> y) (h : a ~> z) : h ≈ fork' f g ↔ (exl' ∘ h ≈ f) * (exr' ∘ h ≈ g) }.

Class Cartesian := { product_obj : obj → obj → obj where "x × y" := (product_obj x y); fork {x y z} (f : x ~> y) (g : x ~> z) : x ~> y × z; exl {x y} : x × y ~> x; exr {x y} : x × y ~> y; fork_respects : ∀ x y z, Proper (equiv ==> equiv ==> equiv) (@fork x y z); ump_products {x y z} (f : x ~> y) (g : x ~> z) (h : x ~> y × z) : h ≈ fork f g ↔ (exl ∘ h ≈ f) * (exr ∘ h ≈ g) }.
Corollary exl_fork {x z w : C} (f : x ~> z) (g : x ~> w) : exl ∘ f △ g ≈ f.  Corollary exr_fork ... : exr ∘ f △ g ≈ g.  Corollary fork_exl_exr {x y : C} : exl △ exr ≈ @id C (x × y).

statement_record.book: A product of X and Y in C is an object X × Y with p_X : X × Y → X and p_Y : X × Y → Y such that for every C with f : C → X and g : C → Y there is a UNIQUE ⟨f,g⟩ : C → X × Y with ⟨f,g⟩ ; p_X = f and ⟨f,g⟩ ; p_Y = g.
statement_record.intree: Class IsCartesianProduct (x y z : C) := { fork' {a} (f : a ~> x) (g : a ~> y) : a ~> z; exl' : z ~> x; exr' : z ~> y; ...; ump_product {a} (f : a ~> x) (g : a ~> y) (h : a ~> z) : h ≈ fork' f g ↔ (exl' ∘ h ≈ f) * (exr' ∘ h ≈ g) }.
statement_record.strength_comparison: same. [IsCartesianProduct x y z] is exactly the book's 'z is a product of x and y' for a DESIGNATED object, so the per-pair reading of Def 3.86 is available and is not merely the bundled 'C has all products'. The ∃! is packaged as a biconditional rather than a Unique record: existence is the given [fork'], and uniqueness is the ← direction (any h satisfying both triangles is ≈ fork' f g); [exl_fork]/[exr_fork] recover the two commuting equations and are proved from it. Setoid rephrasing (≈ for =) is faithful. [Cartesian] is the same UMP with a chosen product operation, plus a Proper field forced by the setoid setting.

Program Definition Cones `(F : J ⟶ C) : Category := {| obj := Cone F; hom := fun N L => { u : vertex_obj[N] ~> vertex_obj[L] & ∀ j, vertex_map[L] ∘ u ≈ @vertex_map _ _ _ F (@coneFrom _ _ _ N) j }; homset := fun _ _ => {| equiv := fun f g => `1 f ≈ `1 g |}; id := fun x => (id; _); compose := fun _ _ _ f g => (`1 f ∘ `1 g; _) |}.

Program Definition Limit_Cones `(F : J ⟶ C) `{T : @Terminal (Cones F)} : Limit F := {| limit_cone := @terminal_obj _ T; ump_limits := fun N => {| unique_obj := `1 (@one _ T N) ; unique_property := `2 (@one _ T N) ; uniqueness := fun v H => @one_unique _ T N (@one _ T N) (v; H) |} |}.
Class Limit `(F : J ⟶ C) := { limit_cone : Cone F; ump_limits : ∀ N : Cone F, ∃! u : N ~> limit_cone, ∀ x : J, vertex_map[limit_cone] ∘ u ≈ @vertex_map _ _ _ _ (@coneFrom _ _ _ N) x }.

statement_record.book: For a diagram D : J → C: a cone (C, c_*) is an object C plus morphisms c_j : C → D(j) with c_k = c_j ; D(f) for every f : j → k; a morphism of cones (C,c_*) → (C',c'_*) is a : C → C' with c_j = a ; c'_j; cones and their morphisms form a category Cone(D); and lim(D) is DEFINED to be the terminal object of Cone(D), its object being the limit object and each c_j the j-th projection.
statement_record.intree: Class ACone (c : obj[C]) (F : J ⟶ C) := { vertex_map (x : J) : c ~> F x; cone_coherence (f : x ~> y) : fmap[F] f ∘ vertex_map x ≈ vertex_map y }; Cones F : Category with hom = { u & ∀ j, vertex_map[L] ∘ u ≈ vertex_map[N] j }; Limit F := { limit_cone : Cone F; ump_limits : ∀ N, ∃! u, ∀ x, vertex_map[limit_cone] ∘ u ≈ vertex_map[N] x }.
statement_record.strength_comparison: same on every clause. [cone_coherence] is literally the book's condition (a) written in ∘-order (D(f) ∘ c_j ≈ c_k for c_k = c_j ; D(f)); the hom of [Cones] is literally the book's cone morphism (one apex map with all leg triangles commuting), with morphism equality taken on the apex map and the commuting witness proof-irrelevant; [vertex_obj] is the limit object and [vertex_map] the j-th projection. One presentational difference, worth naming: the library DEFINES [Limit] by the ∃! universal property rather than literally as the terminal object of [Cones F]; the identification with the book's definition is carried by [Limit_Cones], which proves it only in the direction Terminal (Cones F) ⇒ Limit F (the converse is not in-tree — see 7sketches:3.5.2:ex3.91). Instance/Cones/Comma.v additionally identifies Cones F with the comma category (Δ ↓ =(F)).

statement_record.book: Products are exactly limits in which the indexing category J consists of two objects v, w and no non-identity arrows (the discrete two-object category).
statement_record.intree: Theorem Cartesian_Limit (C : Category) : (∀ F : Two_Discrete ⟶ C, Limit F) ↔ @Cartesian C.
statement_record.strength_comparison: same content, both directions proved (left-to-right reads the limit of [Pick_Two x y] as product_obj/exl/exr/fork; right-to-left builds the limit cone from the product with fork as mediator). One quantifier difference worth naming: the in-tree biconditional is stated at the level of the WHOLE category — 'every two-object discrete diagram has a limit' ⟺ 'C is Cartesian' — rather than per-pair ('this limit cone is a product of x and y'), so a single-pair reading has to be extracted from the proof rather than cited. The general A-indexed analogue is available per-diagram: [limit_is_indexed_product] converts a limit of any discrete diagram into an [IsIndexedProduct] record at its apex, which is the book's claim with J discrete of arbitrary size.
